analysis.investment_thesis: Arvind fails both Magic Formula screens: Earnings Yield of ~7.7% (EBIT 895 Cr / EV ~11,646 Cr) is well below my 12% threshold, and ROCE of 13% sits below the 20% minimum I require for a business worth owning. Zero revenue growth over nine years with exploding capex makes this a capital-intensive, mediocre compounder — exactly the type I avoid.
key_strengths: Debt reduction: borrowings cut from INR 2,640 Cr (2020) to INR 1,537 Cr (2025), improving balance sheet
Consistent positive OCF across all 5 years, averaging ~INR 700 Cr — business does generate cash
Diversified segments (Advanced Materials, technical textiles) offer some differentiation above commodity fabric peers
key_risks: Capex explosion destroying FCF: capex jumped to INR 535 Cr in 2025 (was INR 186 Cr in 2022), FCF collapsed to INR 280 Cr — capex now consuming 60% of EBIT
Nine-year revenue CAGR of 0.4% and EBITDA CAGR of -3.1% — this business has not grown in a decade in real terms
ROE of 9.32% likely below cost of equity — management is destroying value with each incremental rupee of retained capital
red_flags: Capex surge (INR 535 Cr in 2025 vs INR 278 Cr in 2024) with no corresponding revenue growth — CWIP at INR 331 Cr raises questions about returns on new investment
EBIT/EV ~7.7%: earnings yield is below even my minimum acceptable threshold of 12%
Net Profit swung to loss in FY2021 (-27 Cr), signaling cyclical vulnerability; thin 8.5% operating margins leave no margin of safety
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running Arvind through the Magic Formula: EV = market cap INR 10,137 Cr + debt INR 1,562 Cr − cash INR 53 Cr = ~INR 11,646 Cr. EBIT (operating income) FY2025 = INR 895 Cr. Earnings Yield = 7.7% — comfortably below my 12% "attractive" floor. ROCE is disclosed at 13%, confirming the second screen also fails; I need 20%+ to consider a business genuinely good. A textile manufacturer earning 13% on capital at 24x trailing earnings is simply not a Magic Formula candidate — I'm being asked to pay a growth company multiple for a no-growth, capital-intensive operation.

The structural picture is worse on closer inspection. Revenue in 2025 (INR 8,329 Cr) barely exceeds 2016 levels (INR 8,011 Cr) — a 0.4% nine-year CAGR in nominal rupees means real decline. FCF has collapsed from INR 687 Cr (2021) to INR 280 Cr (2025) as capex more than doubled year-on-year to INR 535 Cr. High capex intensity combined with stagnant revenues and sub-cost-of-capital returns is the antithesis of what I look for. Unless this capex cycle generates materially higher ROIC, I see no reason to own Arvind over better-ranked businesses available at similar or cheaper valuations.
